lines.text: When you empty your trash bin, you assume the file is instantly erased from your solid-state drive.
In truth, your operating system never erases data from flash memory: it only removes the file entry from the file system table.
NAND flash has a physical constraint: it can write data in sixteen kilobyte pages, but it can only erase in massive four megabyte blocks.
Because flash cells cannot be overwritten, saving one new file forces the drive to read, erase, and rewrite an entire multi-megabyte block.
Without help, this read-modify-write cycle creates massive write amplification, slashing SSD write speeds by up to eighty percent.
To prevent this, the storage industry created the TRIM command, telling the SSD controller which blocks are dead the moment you delete a file.
TRIM lets the drive controller erase dead flash blocks in the background, keeping write speeds high and preventing premature drive failure.
